sub_units.name: Collections Framework
sub_units.content: The Java Collections Framework (JCF) is a unified architecture for representing and manipulating collections of objects. It provides interfaces (Collection, List, Set, Queue, Map), implementations (ArrayList, HashSet, HashMap, etc.), and algorithms (sorting, searching). The framework reduces programming effort, increases performance, and promotes software reuse. Understanding the collections hierarchy and choosing the right implementation based on requirements like ordering, uniqueness, and performance is fundamental to Java development.

sub_units.name: List & ArrayList
sub_units.content: The List interface represents an ordered collection that allows duplicate elements and provides positional access. ArrayList is the most commonly used List implementation, backed by a dynamic resizable array. It provides O(1) random access by index but O(n) for insertions and deletions in the middle. Key methods include add(), get(), set(), remove(), indexOf(), and subList(). ArrayList is ideal for scenarios requiring frequent read operations and sequential data storage.

sub_units.name: LinkedList & Queue
sub_units.content: LinkedList is a doubly-linked list implementation of both the List and Deque interfaces. It provides O(1) insertions and deletions at both ends but O(n) random access. The Queue interface represents a collection designed for holding elements prior to processing, following FIFO (First-In-First-Out) order. Implementations include LinkedList, PriorityQueue, and ArrayDeque. Key methods include offer(), poll(), peek(), push(), and pop(). Understanding when to use LinkedList vs ArrayList and choosing the right Queue implementation is essential.

sub_units.name: Set & HashSet
sub_units.content: The Set interface represents a collection that does not allow duplicate elements. HashSet is the most commonly used implementation, backed by a HashMap for O(1) average-time add, remove, and contains operations. LinkedHashSet maintains insertion order, while TreeSet stores elements in sorted order using a Red-Black tree. Understanding how hashCode() and equals() affect Set behavior, and choosing between HashSet, LinkedHashSet, and TreeSet based on ordering and performance needs, is critical for effective collection usage.

sub_units.name: Map, HashMap & TreeMap
sub_units.content: The Map interface represents a collection of key-value pairs where each key is unique. HashMap is the most widely used implementation, providing O(1) average-time performance for get and put operations using hashing. TreeMap stores entries in sorted key order using a Red-Black tree with O(log n) operations. LinkedHashMap maintains insertion order. Key methods include put(), get(), containsKey(), keySet(), values(), and entrySet(). Understanding hash collisions, load factors, and choosing the right Map implementation is essential.

sub_units.name: EnumSet & EnumMap
sub_units.content: EnumSet and EnumMap are specialized, high-performance collection implementations designed specifically for use with enum types. EnumSet is a Set implementation that uses a bit vector internally, providing extremely fast operations for enum constants. EnumMap is a Map implementation with enum keys, backed by an array for compact and efficient storage. Both are more efficient than their general-purpose counterparts (HashSet, HashMap) when working with enums and should be preferred in such scenarios.

sub_units.name: Concurrent Collections
sub_units.content: Concurrent collections in Java are thread-safe implementations designed for multi-threaded environments without the performance overhead of synchronized wrappers. Key classes include ConcurrentHashMap (segmented locking for concurrent access), CopyOnWriteArrayList (optimized for read-heavy scenarios), ConcurrentLinkedQueue (lock-free thread-safe queue), and BlockingQueue implementations like ArrayBlockingQueue and LinkedBlockingQueue. These collections are part of the java.util.concurrent package and are essential for building scalable, thread-safe Java applications.

sub_units.name: Generics
sub_units.content: Generics in Java enable type parameterization, allowing classes, interfaces, and methods to operate on specified types while providing compile-time type safety. Generic types eliminate the need for explicit casting and catch type errors at compile time rather than runtime. Key concepts include type parameters (T, E, K, V), bounded types (extends, super), wildcard types (?), generic methods, and type erasure. Understanding generics is essential for writing reusable, type-safe code and working effectively with the Collections Framework.

sub_units.name: Comparable & Comparator
sub_units.content: Comparable and Comparator are interfaces used to define ordering for objects in Java. The Comparable interface defines the natural ordering of a class through the compareTo() method and is implemented by the class itself. The Comparator interface defines custom ordering through the compare() method and is implemented as a separate class or lambda expression. Collections.sort() and Arrays.sort() use these interfaces for sorting. Understanding when to use Comparable vs Comparator is key for flexible and reusable sorting strategies.
